at: Plantation along roadsides to reduce noise pollution
x: A green muffler is 4–5 rows of trees and shrubs planted along roads and near noisy places to absorb noise.
source: NextGen Rocket Environment (src/environment/rocket-environment.txt) p.22 ('Green Muffler – Noise'), p.70

x: Noise is measured in decibels (dB). Celsius and Fahrenheit measure temperature and the dalton measures atomic mass.
source: NextGen Environment APPSC 11 (src/environment/nextgen-environment-appsc-11.txt) p.3 ('Noise is measured in decibels'); NextGen Rocket Environment (src/environment/rocket-environment.txt) p.22

x: Air expands when heated (Charles's law), so a balloon in hot water swells and its volume increases. (Off-topic: physics.)
source: general knowledge, not checked

x: Improperly managed biomedical and e-waste releases toxic substances into soil and water, damaging ecosystems and pushing land-use change. The other options describe benefits, not harm.
source: NextGen Environment APPSC 11 (src/environment/nextgen-environment-appsc-11.txt) p.1 (e-waste and hazardous materials as soil pollutants); Shankar Environment Part 7 (src/environment/shankar-environment-07.ocr.txt) p.1

x: Building materials such as granite, bricks and fly ash carry thorium (with uranium and K-40); the printed and commonly given answer is thorium. Its decay gas radon is what accumulates indoors.
source: https://mcqmate.com/discussion/222089 (same question keyed Thorium); NextGen Environment APPSC 11 (src/environment/nextgen-environment-appsc-11.txt) p.5 (thorium-232 natural radionuclide); PMF Environment Part 4 (src/environment/pmf-environment-04.txt) p.2 (radon seeps into buildings)
evidence: Shankar Environment Part 6 (src/environment/shankar-environment-06.ocr.txt) p.8 (radon from soil confined in poorly ventilated houses)
dispute: Most quiz keys: Thorium. Strictly, the building-material concern that drew public attention is radon-222 (indoor gas from uranium/thorium decay in bricks, granite, soil) – PMF Environment Part 4 p.2; Shankar Part 6 radon note.

x: Newspaper printing inks have contained lead (Pb) compounds, a toxic heavy metal.
source: printed key, not verified; general knowledge, not checked

x: The Supreme Court (2017–18) banned heavy metals such as lead, mercury, arsenic, antimony and lithium, plus barium salts, in firecrackers. Sulphur and potassium nitrate are still standard cracker ingredients.
source: printed key, not verified; general knowledge, not checked

x: Treating waste before dumping, minimising pesticides and crop rotation all control soil pollution. Setting up watersheds is a soil and water conservation step, not a soil-pollution control, so only ii is the answer.
source: Shankar Environment Part 7 (src/environment/shankar-environment-07.ocr.txt) p.2 (control measures: reduce chemicals, biofertilisers, solid-waste treatment); app notes 5:102 (old-notes.txt) sub 1 (watersheds not a control, APPSC 2019)

x: Bioremediation is used mainly to clean contaminated soil (and groundwater), using microbes or plants to break down oil, pesticides and solvents. It is not a tool for noise, air or waterborne disease.
source: NextGen Environment APPSC 13 (src/environment/nextgen-environment-appsc-13.txt) p.2, p.6 (microbes treat land contaminated by pesticides, oil, solvents); NextGen Rocket Environment (src/environment/rocket-environment.txt) p.63

x: The Noise Pollution (Regulation and Control) Rules, 2000 ban loudspeakers and public address systems from 10 pm to 6 am, except in closed premises. The Rules are framed under the EP Act, but the prohibition itself is in the Rules.
source: PMF Environment Part 4 (src/environment/pmf-environment-04.txt) p.2 (Noise Rules 2000 under EPA 1986); Shankar Environment Part 7 (src/environment/shankar-environment-07.ocr.txt) p.2 (night 10 pm–6 am)

x: Frequency is set by the vibrating source and stays the same in any medium. Speed and wavelength change with the medium. (Off-topic: physics of sound.)
source: general knowledge, not checked

x: Under the Noise Rules, 2000 the residential limit is 55 dB(A) by day and 45 dB(A) by night. 75 dB is the industrial day limit.
source: Shankar Environment Part 7 (src/environment/shankar-environment-07.ocr.txt) p.2 (zone table: residential 55/45)

x: Capillaries are the narrowest blood vessels (about 5–10 micrometres), one cell thick. (Off-topic: biology.)
source: general knowledge, not checked

x: Crackers louder than 125 dB(AI) or 145 dB(C)pk at 4 m from the point of bursting may not be made, sold or used (EP Rules standard, amended 2006).

x: The decibel measures noise. The cusec measures water flow, magnitude measures earthquakes or star brightness, and the kilometre measures distance.
source: NextGen Environment APPSC 11 (src/environment/nextgen-environment-appsc-11.txt) p.3

x: Trees give shade and moderate local climate, improve soil and give income and food. Absorbing noise from small industries and irrigation is not counted as a benefit of tree planting for poor communities.
source: printed key, not verified (APPSC AEE 2023, passage-style)

x: The decibel (dB) is a logarithmic unit of sound intensity (loudness level), not of electricity, light or heat.

x: Green mufflers are rows of trees and shrubs that absorb noise, so they act against noise pollution.

x: The sone is the unit of perceived loudness. The decibel measures sound level, the phon measures loudness level and the hertz measures frequency.

x: Noise is measured in decibels (dB). The hertz measures frequency and the nanometre is a unit of length.

x: A green muffler is a belt of trees and shrubs that absorbs noise; it also traps some dust and gases, but it is a noise-pollution control.

x: Hearing loss is measured in decibels (dB HL on an audiogram), the same unit as sound level.
source: NextGen Environment APPSC 11 (src/environment/nextgen-environment-appsc-11.txt) p.3 (noise measured in dB; >75 dB prolonged → hearing loss)

x: Argon, neon and helium are constituents of air. Radon is radioactive and short-lived, so it is taken as the noble gas not present in air. (Off-topic: chemistry.)
source: general knowledge, not checked; PMF Environment Part 4 (src/environment/pmf-environment-04.txt) p.2 (radon is released from rocks and soil)
evidence: NextGen Environment APPSC 11 (src/environment/nextgen-environment-appsc-11.txt) p.5 (radon-222 a natural radionuclide in the crust)
dispute: Most books: all noble gases except radon occur in air. Strictly, radon is present in trace amounts near the ground (decay of radium in soil).

x: Radioactive pollution causes hereditary (genetic) changes and cancer (carcinogenesis). Mineral imbalance in soil and hindered blood circulation are not its recognised effects, so I and IV is the answer.
source: NextGen Rocket Environment (src/environment/rocket-environment.txt) p.63 ('Radioactive pollution – Hereditary changes + carcinogenesis'); NextGen Environment APPSC 11 (src/environment/nextgen-environment-appsc-11.txt) p.6 (genetic mutations, cancers)
evidence: Shankar Environment Part 7 (src/environment/shankar-environment-07.ocr.txt) p.5 (long-range effects: mutations, tumours, cancer)
dispute: Printed key: I, III and IV. Rocket Environment p.63 gives radioactive pollution → hereditary changes + carcinogenesis (I and IV).
